title: Meet my friend
goal: Introduce other people, say what they do and where they live, and tell apart two ways of saying "he/she/it is": c'est and il est.
bekal: introduce a third person with *voici* and *je te présente*
state a job without an article: *il est professeur*
tell *c'est* (pointing someone out) from *il est* (describing them)

dialogs.title: Dialogue — À la cafétéria
dialogs.intro: Camille introduces Budi to her friend in the campus cafeteria.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Budi, je te présente Thomas. C'est un ami.
lines.id: Budi, this is Thomas. He's a friend.
lines.literal: Budi, I to-you present Thomas. it-is a friend.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Hi Thomas, nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: Thomas:
lines.text: Enchanté. Tu es dans la classe de Camille ?
lines.id: Nice to meet you too. Are you in Camille's class?
lines.literal: enchanted. you you-are in the class of Camille?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Oui, on est ensemble. Et toi, tu es étudiant ?
lines.id: Yes, we're in it together. And you, are you a student?
lines.literal: yes, one is together. and you, you you-are student?

lines.speaker: Thomas:
lines.text: Non, je travaille. Je suis architecte.
lines.id: No, I work. I'm an architect.
lines.literal: no, I I-work. I I-am architect.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ah, c'est intéressant ! Tu habites à Lyon ?
lines.id: Oh, that's interesting! Do you live in Lyon?
lines.literal: ah, it-is interesting! you you-live in Lyon?

lines.speaker: Thomas:
lines.text: Oui, j'habite ici depuis trois ans. Et toi ?
lines.id: Yes, I've lived here for three years. And you?
lines.literal: yes, I-live here since three years. and you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Moi, je suis ici depuis deux semaines seulement.
lines.id: I've only been here for two weeks.
lines.literal: me, I I-am here since two weeks only.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Il parle déjà bien français, non ?
lines.id: His French is already good, isn't it?
lines.literal: he speaks already well French, no?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Merci ! Mais je fais encore beaucoup de fautes.
lines.id: Thanks! But I still make lots of mistakes.
lines.literal: thanks! but I make still much of mistakes.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Ce n'est pas grave. C'est normal !
lines.literal: that not-is not serious. it-is normal!

notes: **Jobs take no article.** *Je suis architecte*, not *je suis un architecte*. This is one of the few places where French drops its article — and exactly where English speakers tend to add one (*I am an architect*).

**On is used for "we".** Grammatically *on* means "one" and takes the same verb form as *il/elle*, but in everyday speech it almost always means *nous*. *On est ensemble* = we're together. *Nous* sounds more formal; on the street, French people say *on*.

**Depuis = since/for, and the sentence stays in the present.** *J'habite ici depuis trois ans* — literally "I live here since three years". English uses "I have lived", but French uses the plain present.
**J'habite, not je habite.** When the verb starts with a vowel or a silent h, *je* is cut to *j'*. The same happens with *le → l'*, *ne → n'*, *de → d'*. French doesn't like two vowels colliding.
**Non? at the end of a sentence** is the lightest way to ask for agreement, like "right?" or "isn't it?" in English. Its more common relatives: *n'est-ce pas ?* and, in casual talk, *hein ?*

**Beaucoup de fautes**, not *beaucoup fautes*. After quantity words like *beaucoup*, *peu*, *assez*, *trop*, French always slips in **de** and drops the article. This rule comes back in full in Unit 12.

**Ce n'est pas grave** is literally "it's not serious" — the most useful phrase in all of French. It is used to forgive, to reassure, and to close an awkward moment. The short street form: *c'est pas grave*.

grammars.title: C'est or il est?
body: Both translate as "he/she is" or "it is", and learners almost always pick the wrong one. The dividing line is simple: look at the word that follows.
after: A shortcut that rarely fails: **an article after it → c'est**. No article → *il est*.
The plurals are *ce sont* (*ce sont mes amis*) and *ils sont* (*ils sont étudiants*). In conversation, *ce sont* is often replaced by plain *c'est*.

grammars.title: -er verbs, the first group
body: Nine out of ten French verbs end in **-er**, and they all behave the same way. Drop the -er and add the endings below.
after: ⚠️ Four forms — *parle, parles, parle, parlent* — sound **exactly the same**: PAHRL. The endings *-es* and *-ent* are completely silent. Only *parlons* and *parlez* actually sound different.
Which means your ear can never tell *il parle* from *ils parlent*. The pronoun makes the difference — and that is why pronouns can never be dropped in French.
Other verbs that behave the same way and are useful right away: *travailler* (to work), *aimer* (to like), *étudier* (to study), *regarder* (to watch), *écouter* (to listen), *manger* (to eat).

blocks.text: French has three levels of formality for something as simple as introducing a friend. Choose according to who you are talking to, not who is being introduced.

head: Sentence
Pronunciation
Used with
rows: People you address politely, or more than one person

blocks.text: The standard reply is *enchanté(e)*. In a relaxed setting, *bonjour* plus your own name is enough. In everyday conversation French people often just answer *salut*.

blocks.title: The jobs you'll name most often
items: *étudiant / étudiante* (student), *professeur* (teacher, lecturer — the same for women), *médecin* (doctor), *ingénieur* (engineer), *architecte* (architect).
*infirmier / infirmière* (nurse), *serveur / serveuse* (waiter / waitress), *vendeur / vendeuse* (salesperson), *cuisinier / cuisinière* (cook), *employé / employée* (employee).
Remember: no article after *être*. But with an article after *c'est* — *c'est un médecin*.
